title: The written Kasem alphabet
summary: Use a, e, i, o, u, ɛ and ɔ as the seven written vowel symbols. Consonant symbols are b, ch, d, f, g, j, k, l, m, n, ny, ŋ, p, r, s, t, v, w, y, z and h (the book brackets h). Use ŋ instead of the old ng symbol, j instead of dʒ, and ch instead of tʃ. The book rejects ɣ. The sounds written phonetically as ɩ, ʋ and ə do not require those letters in ordinary writing.

title: Seven symbols represent ten vowel sounds
summary: Write /a/ as a, /ɛ/ as ɛ, /i/ as i, /u/ as u and /ɔ/ as ɔ. Write /ɩ/ as e and /ʋ/ as o. Write /e/ as ei and /o/ as wo, subject to the rules for long vowels and repeated vowels. Phonetic spellings are pronunciation descriptions, not replacement headwords.

title: Writing the central vowel
summary: For /ɜ/ or [ə], write ei in a one-syllable consonant-vowel word; write oa after a labialised consonant in a one-syllable word; write ei in the first syllable of a two-syllable word; write a in the last syllable of a word with two or more syllables. This depends on the word's sound and syllable position, so a global replacement of ə is insufficient.

title: Keep different vowel sounds distinguishable
summary: The revised spelling distinguishes words that older conventions wrote alike: doŋo is new and dwoŋo is old; pogo is husk and pwogo is nest; kogo is feather, kwogo is zombi and kugu is maize cob. Do not merge words because an older spelling or an ASCII search form looks alike.

title: Write vowel length by doubling
summary: Double the vowel symbol for a long vowel: daa, bii, lɔɔ and tuu. Long /o/ is woo. Long /e/ is ee rather than eei; the book writes teeni for trees and lwooru for beggar.

title: Vowel digraphs in words with several syllables
summary: When /o/ occurs several times in a word, only its first occurrence is wo: bworo and kwolo. When /e/ occurs several times, only its final occurrence is ei: lelei. These rules depend on the vowel sounds, not on blindly replacing every written e or o.

title: Include w for labialised consonants
summary: Represent consonant labialisation with w, rather than inserting u and making a one-syllable word look like two syllables. The book allows w combinations with consonants except r, including bw, chw, dw, fw, gw, jw, kw, lw, mw, nw, nyw, ŋw, pw, sw, tw, vw, yw and zw. Its correct spellings distinguish sua, swoa, soa, swa, swei and swi.

title: Write words fully even when speech reduces them
summary: Write the full word rather than its fast-speech reduction. This makes different words easier to distinguish. Keep internal vowels as well: write dindeilimi for tongue, lɔgese, tigisi and zamese rather than the shortened pronunciations.

title: Nouns and determiners are separate words
summary: Spell both the noun and its determiner fully and separately even when they merge in pronunciation. The book gives naane dem, chechare dem and yeili dem. Determiners must not be described as inseparable pieces of every noun.

title: Verbs and ordinary objects are separate words
summary: Keep verbs fully spelt and separate from ordinary noun objects, including Kale naane and pare tampɔgɔ. With object pronouns such as o and m, spell the verb fully and attach the pronoun using a hyphen: zeili-o, mage-o, bwei-o and bwoi-o.

title: Preserve the full forms of nasal-final pronunciations
summary: Some words genuinely end in m, including dɔɔm, diim, kam, kom, bam, sem, yeim and zem. Other words only sound shortened in speech: write lane, bane, ywoni, saleme and badwoŋi fully. Keep the final vowel in saŋe, vaŋe, jwoŋi and tɔŋe.

title: Word division
summary: Write nouns separately from determiners, subject pronouns separately from verbs, verbs separately from ordinary objects, and numerals as independent words. Tense and aspect markers are also separate words. Object pronouns attached by a hyphen are the stated verb-object exception.

title: Noun and adjective compounds use a hyphen
summary: When an adjective qualifies a noun, the noun loses its suffix and the adjective keeps its full form. Hyphenate the compound: nɔn-kukula, na-nia, ka-jworo and na-digiru. Spacing or joining everything without a hyphen can obscure the meaning.

title: Hyphenate compounds with nyeno and nyena
summary: Use a hyphen in compounds ending with nyeno or nyena: nankɔ-nyeno, bɛyer-nyeno and wolon-nyeno. The similar element tu remains a separate word, as in teo tu and podea tu. The source's nandɔɔro to nankɔ example is retained as printed rather than treated as a productive spelling conversion.
examples: political leader or head of state

title: Verb and deverbative compounds
summary: Noun-verb or verb-noun compounds can be written as one word, with or without a hyphen. The book pairs nɔntora with nɔn-tora, golesɔla with gole-sɔla, kadiri with ka-diri and kedia with ke-dia.

title: Names and nominalised clauses
summary: A sentence used as a personal name is written as a single name: Ajegedawe. For other clauses or phrases functioning as words, separate constituents with hyphens: Ka-nyɔ-na-ka-ve-muni and Ka-yiŋi-daani.

title: Write opaque compounds together
summary: When a compound has a meaning different from the ordinary combination of its parts, write it together. Manlaataŋa means rainbow; manlaa taŋa means the chameleon's bow. Digabu and tiabu mean cat; diga bu means one's child.

title: Use diacritics only in the specified cases
summary: Do not use nasal tildes or vowel-quality diacritics. Ordinary words do not need every tone marked. The book prescribes a limited set of tone distinctions: á, dé, wó, yé and deém, with occasional véi/vèi distinctions. The book provides acute and grave marks, not a general mid-tone macron.

title: Distinguish plural á and dé from a and de
summary: Write á for second-person plural subject you, and a for first-person singular I. Write dé for first-person plural we; write de without that mark for the class II pronoun. The pronoun appendix has conflicting forms; these explicit tone rules control the keyboard shortcuts.

title: Distinguish positive wó from negative wo
summary: Use wó for the positive future marker and wo for the negative marker. They occur in the same position, so the written tone distinguishes their meanings.

title: Distinguish yé from ye
summary: Write yé for the negative imperative and ye for the negative subjunctive. The book distinguishes saying that someone should not eat from commanding them not to eat.
examples: he/she said Adoa shouldn't eat it
he/she commanded Adoa not to eat it

title: Future negative baa has a long vowel
summary: Write the future negative as baa, without a required tone mark; its doubled vowel distinguishes it from imperfective negative ba.

title: The source's conditional na examples are ambiguous
summary: The book discusses conditional na and a subordinator pronounced ná, but tells the reader to write both as na and prints identical Kasem examples with different English meanings. Preserve this limitation; this document alone does not settle how to distinguish the two written clauses.
note: The identical source examples are retained in the reference, with an ambiguity notice. They are not presented as unambiguous sentence translations.

title: Long ago deém differs from last year deem
summary: Write deém for long ago and deem for last year.
examples: Adoa made a farm a long time ago
Adoa made a farm last year

title: Occasional tone distinctions on vei
summary: When necessary, write véi for the imperative go, vèi for the past went, and vei for going or intending to go. These are specified distinctions, not permission to place arbitrary accents on every vowel.
examples: Adoa is going or intends to go to market.

title: Kasem grammatical terminology
summary: The appendix provides Kasem equivalents for grammar, sentence, clause, phrase, word, morpheme, subject, predicator, complement, adjunct, noun, pronoun, adjective, adverb, determiner, linker, ideophone, verb, syllable, phone, consonant and vowel. Some terms are adapted borrowings; the full list is searchable in the dictionary.

title: Simple pronouns by person and noun class
summary: The pronoun table lists non-emphatic and emphatic forms for singular and plural persons and classes I–V. Class agreement changes third-person forms. The full table is retained. Its second-person plural à and third-person emphatic amo differ from other parts of the document; consult the explicit tone rules and do not infer corrections to every cell.

title: Counting forms and class agreement
summary: The book lists cardinal counting forms kalo/dedoa, nle, ntɔ, nna, nnu, ndo, npae, nana, nogobo/nogo and fuga. Its ordinal/agreement table combines singular de-, ka-, ko- with -doa, -dwe, -doo and plural ba-, ya-, sɛ-, te-, de- with -lei, -tɔ and -na by noun class. Multiplicative forms include bedwe, bilei, betɔ, bena, binu, beredo and nerepae (berepɛ). Keep the table's labels and class scope rather than assuming one universal form per number.
